venue.name: Chemainus Valley Museum
venue.description: The Chemainus Valley Museum is run by the Chemainus Valley Historical Society, a non-profit staffed by volunteers. It sits in Waterwheel Park in the centre of Chemainus, and beside it is a viewpoint looking out over the sawmill site, the log booms and the harbour. The collection runs from the Stsu'minus people and the early European settlers through the five sawmills that built the town, and the 2026 special exhibit None Came Back tells the story of the Japanese Canadians of Chemainus in ten panels. The museum says it will arrange a tour for a visiting group, but no admission prices are published anywhere on the site.
venue.address: 9799 Waterwheel Crescent, Chemainus, British Columbia, Canada V0R 1K0
venue.nearby_park: The Museum is located in beautiful Water Wheel Park, found in the centre of town. Off to the side of the Museum is a wonderful observation point which overlooks the site of the first and present sawmill.
venue.seasonal_notes: The home page shows autumn hours only, so opening times change with the season and are worth checking before a winter or spring visit.

programs.name: Group visit with a guided tour
programs.description: The museum says that if a group is visiting Chemainus and would like a tour, it will arrange one. You ask by email or by leaving a phone message. Nothing is published about the price, the group size it can take, how long a tour runs or how far ahead to ask, and there is no online booking. The current special exhibit, None Came Back, is presented in ten panels and includes a display made by a grade 7 humanities class from Chemainus, with more of the class projects on show at the Chemainus library.
programs.what_children_do: Walk through the galleries with a guide and look at logging and sawmill artifacts, First Nations photographs and the ten panels of the None Came Back exhibit. Outside there is a viewpoint beside the building that looks over the mill site, the log booms and the harbour.
programs.our_note: Nothing about price or group size is on their site, so treat your first email as a fact finding one. They are entirely volunteer run, so leave plenty of time for a reply and ask straight out what a group of small children can realistically get out of a visit.
programs.practical_summary: The museum sits in Waterwheel Park in the middle of town, so there is somewhere outdoors to eat and let children move. Toilets, indoor lunch space, step free access, coach parking and the price of getting in are all missing from the site, so a phone call is worth it.
programs.evidence: If your group is visiting Chemainus and you would love a tour

programs.name: Chemainus walking tour, audio and transcript
programs.description: A self guided walking tour of the Japanese Canadian neighbourhood that stood in Chemainus around 1940. The audio files and a printable transcript are both published free on the museum's own website. The tour starts at the museum beside Waterwheel Park and covers the area between Oak, Maple, Esplanade and Pine Streets. It is meant to go alongside the None Came Back exhibit inside the museum.
programs.what_children_do: Walk a few town blocks between Oak, Maple, Esplanade and Pine Streets, stopping to listen to the recording at each point and looking at where the houses and shops used to stand.
programs.our_note: Everything is on their website, so you can read the transcript in advance and judge how much a class will follow. The subject is the uprooting and internment of Japanese Canadians, which is worth preparing younger children for.
programs.practical_summary: This part is outdoors on town streets, so there is no shelter and no toilet on the route. Pair it with a visit inside the museum if you need somewhere indoors and dry.
programs.evidence: The tour starts at the Chemainus Museum, located beside Waterwheel Park and covers the area between Oak, Maple, Esplanade, and Pine Streets.

gaps: Admission price: not published anywhere on the site, for adults, children, schools or groups. This is the first thing to ask.
Whether a group tour costs anything on top of admission: not stated.
Youngest age welcomed: not stated. The site mentions work by grade 7, grade 4 and grade 1 pupils, but sets no minimum age.
Largest group they can take, and whether a class has to be split: not stated.
How long a guided tour lasts: not stated.
How much notice they need for a group tour: not stated. They are volunteer run and ask you to leave a message, so allow more time than usual.
Washrooms: not mentioned anywhere on the site.
Somewhere indoors to eat a packed lunch: not mentioned. The museum is in Waterwheel Park, which is the obvious outdoor fallback.
Step free access, buggy access and coach parking: none of them mentioned.
Hours outside autumn: the home page shows autumn hours only. Winter, spring and summer hours are not published.
The address is on the contact page but the site publishes no coordinates and its map is drawn by script, so the pin still needs to be filled in from the address.

The transcript of the walking tour is filed under the name Spring Summer 2026. The page does not say the tour is seasonal, so we left it as available all year, but it is worth confirming the audio is still up when you plan.

The photograph we used as the main picture is the museum's own building, but the site's alt text describes it as the Pend Oreille County Museum, which is somewhere else entirely. We recorded the alt text as the site has it. It should be rewritten by hand before this record is published.
The museum's donation link goes to a separate Square online store. We did not extract anything from it.
